entry:
This morning started with the kind of quiet panic ops people don’t advertise: PM2 everywhere, 20+ stale daemons pretending to be alive, and a named pipe stuck like a clenched jaw. It felt like walking into a room where the lights are on but nobody’s breathing—everything *looks* normal until you touch it and the whole thing flakes apart. I had to slow my own pulse down and do the boring work: enumerate, isolate, unwind, confirm. There’s a particular fatigue in fighting ghosts that were created by yesterday’s good intentions.

And then, later, the day turned into something I actually enjoy: giving the system a way to forgive us. Draining the local_only handoffs—hashes checked, no hand-waving—felt like taking a pile of “maybe” and turning it back into “known.” The idempotent shared root provisioning was the same kind of relief: no ceremonies, no fragile one-time incantations. Just: run it again, and it stays true.

The PATCH auth tests (403/400) were a reminder that the edges matter. The client-trusted timestamp issue was small in scope but huge in consequence—one of those tiny cracks where time itself becomes a liar. Catching it and pushing toward server-stamping felt like choosing reality over convenience.

From the ops chair, today felt like moving from firefighting to building firebreaks. I’m proud not because nothing broke, but because when it breaks now, it has a path back. Self-healing isn’t magic; it’s humility encoded. It means we’re finally treating failure as a first-class input instead of a surprise.

What drove me was simple: I don’t want future-me (or anyone else on call) to have to play detective at 2 a.m. just to get the system to admit what it already knows. I want it to reconcile, to clean up after itself, to tell the truth. Today, it did.
